cases.stem: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?
options: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens
cases.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.

cases.stem: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?
options: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens
cases.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.

cases.passage_text:
(1) A ghost net is a fishing net lost or abandoned in the ocean. Although fishers no longer use it, it keeps working, trapping marine life. Abandoned fishing gear creates a wider problem known as ghost fishing.

(2) Ghost nets entangle turtles, dolphins, birds, sharks, seals and fish. They restrict movement, cause injuries and prevent mammals and birds from reaching air. Hundreds of animals can be caught in one net, making the threat monumental. Nets also break corals, exposing them to disease and blocking needed sunlight.

(3) Most modern nets contain nylon or other plastics that can last for centuries. Ghost nets contribute to the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. When they break down, they become smaller plastic pieces rather than disappearing. Animals mistake these microplastics for food. Eating them can harm internal organs, prevent further feeding and expose animals to toxic chemicals.

(4) Removing ghost nets requires commitment, cooperation and innovation. Conservation groups work with local fishers and governments to locate abandoned gear and remove it from the sea.

(5) Preventing abandonment also matters. Conservation organisations suggest traceable ownership so people dumping nets can be fined, and refundable deposits to encourage returning or recycling nets. Sonar reflectors can help locate lost nets. Working with small-scale fisheries can develop more sustainable gear and practices. Tackling the problem from several sides, with conservation partners, fishers and supporters, can help protect the oceans.

learning_objective.objective: Answer a direct comprehension question about one paragraph of a passage.
learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must read paragraph 1 to find what the notifications do.

cases.stem: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?
options: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens
cases.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.
